title: Hot Cross Buns
subtitle: Spiced, fruited yeasted buns with a white cross
excerpt: The traditional British Easter bun: a soft, enriched dough scented with mixed spice and cinnamon, packed with dried fruit and orange zest, marked with a flour paste cross and glazed with syrup straight from the oven.

recipe.sourceNotes: Hot cross buns are associated in Britain with Good Friday, when they are traditionally baked and eaten to mark the end of Lent. The cross on the bun is a Christian symbol, and the association of spiced buns with Easter predates the Reformation: a royal edict of 1592 attempted to restrict spiced buns to Good Friday, Christmas, and funerals, suggesting they were already widely made and eaten. The modern bun is a soft, enriched, yeasted dough with mixed spice and dried fruit; the cross is traditionally made from a flour and water paste piped onto the dough before baking, then glazed with sugar syrup or apricot jam after baking. Thomas Reckitt's recipe of 1733 is one of the earliest written records.

content.text: Use strong bread flour for the best texture: the higher gluten content gives the buns their characteristic soft but springy crumb. The dough is enriched with butter, egg, and milk, which makes it slower to prove than a plain bread dough. Do not hurry the proves: the second prove in particular determines the final open texture of the bun. The flour paste for the crosses should be piped immediately before the buns go into the oven.

items.preparation: plus extra for the cross paste

content.text: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar, spices, and salt. Rub in the butter to fine crumbs. Make a well and add the beaten egg and warm milk. Mix to a dough, then knead for 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Knead in the dried fruit, currants, and orange zest. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and leave to rise for 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled.

Knock back the dough and divide into 12 equal pieces (about 100 g each). Shape each into a smooth ball. Arrange close together on lined baking trays. Cover and prove for 45 minutes to 1 hour until puffed and touching.

Heat the oven to 200 C (180 C fan). For the crosses: mix 75 g of plain flour with 5 to 6 tablespoons of water to a thick, smooth paste. Transfer to a piping bag with a small nozzle and pipe crosses onto the top of each bun. Bake for 18 to 20 minutes until golden brown.

For the glaze: dissolve 2 tablespoons of caster sugar in 2 tablespoons of boiling water. Brush over the buns the moment they come out of the oven. Eat warm on the day of baking; toast split halves on subsequent days.
